reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: Progressive loss of subcutaneous fat over much of the body developing during childhood or adolescence in a previously normal individual
Often follows or accompanies a panniculitis, an autoimmune disorder, or is idiopathic, suggesting immune-mediated destruction of adipose tissue
Widespread fat loss lowers leptin and drives ectopic lipid deposition with severe insulin resistance, acanthosis nigricans, hypertriglyceridaemia, and hepatic steatosis
Insulin-resistant diabetes commonly emerges, and hepatomegaly from steatosis may progress to steatohepatitis
Screening for associated autoimmune disease (including autoimmune hepatitis and thyroid disease) is worthwhile given the immune association
Leptin (metreleptin) replacement benefits the more leptin-deficient patients, improving triglycerides, glycaemia, and hepatic fat
Distinguishing acquired from congenital generalised lipodystrophy relies on documenting normal earlier body fat and later-onset loss
Diagnosis combines the generalised acquired fat-loss pattern, low leptin, the metabolic panel, and exclusion of a genetic cause
reference.pathophysiology: Acquired generalised lipodystrophy is a non-inherited, usually immune-mediated loss of adipose tissue across the body in someone who previously had normal fat. It is frequently preceded by a panniculitis or associated with autoimmune conditions, implicating immune-driven adipocyte destruction, though many cases are idiopathic. As functional fat is lost, leptin falls and lipid can no longer be stored appropriately, overflowing into liver and muscle to cause severe insulin resistance. The consequent metabolic picture mirrors congenital generalised lipodystrophy, with hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis, acanthosis nigricans, and insulin-resistant diabetes.
additionalDifferentials: Severe systemic illness with cachexia or wasting
Poorly controlled diabetes with generalised weight loss
additionalInvestigations: Serum leptin (typically low) and fasting insulin/C-peptide
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging for steatosis, with consideration of autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune screen (including thyroid antibodies) given frequent immune associations
Whole-body or regional fat imaging to document the generalised deficit
Genetic testing where needed to exclude a congenital generalised form
redFlags: Coexisting active autoimmune disease requiring its own treatment
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends on metabolic control and any underlying autoimmune disease; leptin (metreleptin) replacement and vigorous management of triglycerides and glucose improve outcomes, but progressive liver disease and pancreatitis are significant threats if untreated.
pitfalls: Mistaking acquired disease for a congenital form and missing the immune/panniculitis association
Overlooking an associated autoimmune disorder such as autoimmune hepatitis
Underestimating pancreatitis risk with very high triglycerides
Assuming conventional insulin doses will control severe insulin-resistant diabetes
Failing to reassess leptin status when deciding on replacement therapy
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on lipodystrophy
management: Metreleptin (recombinant leptin) replacement in the more leptin-deficient patients to improve glycaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia and hepatic steatosis
Low-fat diet to limit chylomicronaemia and ectopic lipid deposition
Treat insulin-resistant diabetes with metformin and, where required, high-dose insulin, alongside triglyceride-lowering with fibrates and omega-3 fatty acids
Screen for and treat associated autoimmune disease such as autoimmune hepatitis and thyroid disease, with immunosuppression where indicated
Surveillance for progression to steatohepatitis and for acute pancreatitis driven by severe hypertriglyceridaemia
Multidisciplinary care spanning endocrinology, hepatology and dietetics
